item.description:

Short Description:
Unified product catalog and integration guide for 50+ Cisco products in Splunk — find the right add-ons, check compatibility, and streamline deployment across Enterprise and Cloud.


Description:
Splunk Cisco App Navigator (SCAN) is the front door to the Cisco–Splunk ecosystem. It provides a unified product catalog of 50+ Cisco integrations with interactive cards that show which Splunk add-ons are available for each product, along with platform compatibility, sourcetype coverage, real-time data-flow detection, deployment guidance, and direct links to Splunkbase and documentation. SCAN solves a persistent problem for Splunk administrators and Cisco engineers: figuring out which Cisco add-ons to install, whether they are compatible with your Splunk version and platform (Enterprise or Cloud), whether the data is actually flowing, and how the pieces fit together. Instead of searching Splunkbase and cross-referencing documentation manually, SCAN puts everything in one place and validates it against your live environment. The interactive catalog is organized across Security, Networking, Observability, and Collaboration with 19 subcategories. Each card shows required add-ons, sourcetype counts, integration badges for SC4S, NetFlow, Enterprise Security, SOAR, and ITSI, version intelligence, and live data-flow status — a single search validates 320 sourcetypes at once so every card knows whether data is actually arriving. Beyond the catalog, SCAN ships an Ecosystem Intelligence dashboard for portfolio analytics, Indexer Tier Detection that validates add-ons are deployed on the correct tier in clustered deployments, a Magic Eight Audit that deep-inspects props.conf parsing settings to catch ingestion problems early, context-aware integration guidance modals for SC4S, NetFlow/IPFIX, Enterprise Security, SOAR, and ITSI, and pre-built reports covering catalog analysis, sourcetype coverage, compatibility, and deployment readiness. SCAN is fully theme-aware with a three-state toggle (Light, Dark, Auto) and is designed for Splunk administrators, Cisco sales engineers, partner teams, and anyone who needs to navigate the Cisco–Splunk integration landscape quickly and confidently.

Splunk App for Secure Networking helps organizations turn fragmented Cisco infrastructure, networking, identity, security, application experience, and building telemetry into clear executive and operational insights in Splunk. Cisco environments often produce data across multiple products, add-ons, indexes, sourcetypes, and data models. Building a consolidated view normally requires teams to create and maintain separate searches, dashboards, index mappings, and visualizations. This app provides a reusable foundation that brings those signals together through configurable dashboards, shared search definitions, index-mapping macros, health indicators, drilldowns, and interactive topology views. It visualizes data already ingested into Splunk through applicable Cisco add-ons, integrations, and data models. The dashboards displayed and populated in each environment depend on the available data sources. The app is intended for network operations, security operations, IT operations, Splunk administrators, architects, customer success teams, and executives who need a consolidated view of the health, security, availability, and performance of their Cisco environment.

item.description:

Release Notes:
**Splunk MCP Server 2.0.0** Splunk MCP Server 2.0.0 adds tools for investigating alerts and discovering sourcetypes. It also introduces paginated results, improved MCP and OAuth compatibility, stronger security for custom tools, and enhanced telemetry. **What's New** **Alert Investigation** Added six tools for investigating Splunk alerts: * splunk\_list\_alerts * splunk\_get\_alert\_details * splunk\_list\_fired\_alerts * splunk\_get\_fired\_alert\_details * splunk\_get\_alert\_throttle * splunk\_list\_active\_throttles Use these tools to find alerts, investigate fired alerts, and view configured or active alert throttles. **Sourcetype Discovery** * Added the splunk\_get\_sourcetypes tool for discovering sourcetypes that contain indexed data. * Results include event counts, time coverage, indexes, and configuration details. You can filter results by index and time range. **Paginated Results** Added pagination to the following tools: * splunk\_get\_indexes * splunk\_get\_sourcetypes * splunk\_list\_alerts * splunk\_list\_fired\_alerts * splunk\_get\_fired\_alert\_details * splunk\_list\_active\_throttles Paginated responses include the total number of results, offset, and page size. They also follow the configured default and maximum row limits. **MCP and OAuth Improvements** * Improved MCP-compatible tool error responses. * Added the openid scope to OAuth discovery. * Added the openWorldHint annotation to all built-in tools. **Search and Splunk AI Assistant Improvements** * Increased the maximum prompt and query length to 10,000 characters for splunk\_run\_query and Splunk AI Assistant tools. * Changed the default splunk\_run\_query time range from 24 hours to 6 hours. **Issues Fixed** * Fixed saved search arguments that contain escaped nested quotes. * Fixed an incompatible authentication scheme used by detached searches. * Improved error messages for missing MCP capabilities, search timeouts, and Splunk AI Assistant data discovery tool. **Upgrade Considerations** * splunk\_get\_metadata no longer supports sourcetype discovery. Use splunk\_get\_sourcetypes instead. * Calls to splunk\_run\_query without a time range now search the last 6 hours instead of the last 24 hours. * splunk\_get\_indexes now returns paginated results and uses name instead of title for the index identifier. * The Splunk AI Assistant data discovery tool requires Splunk AI Assistant 2.2.0 or later with Agent Mode enabled.


Description:
MCP Server for Splunk Platform The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard and framework that enables seamless, secure, and standardized two-way communication between AI applications (like large language models) and external data sources or tools. It acts as a universal adapter allowing AI systems to access, execute, and integrate functionalities from diverse systems through a common protocol, simplifying data sharing and tool interoperability without custom coding for each integration. Splunk's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server leverages this to provide a standardized, secure, and scalable interface to connect AI assistants, agents, and other intelligent systems with data in the Splunk platform for both Enterprise & Cloud customers in beta. 🔑 Key Features - Universal Connectivity Seamlessly connects AI agents and tools to Splunk data resources in a secure and efficient manner. - Enterprise-Grade Security Includes built-in authentication, authorization, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). - Rapid Deployment Offers a plug-and-play solution, eliminating the need for custom integrations. ⚙️ Core Capabilities - Explore the Data Navigate and interact with Splunk data effortlessly. - Discover Knowledge Objects Identify and access relevant saved searches, lookups, and other knowledge assets. - Execute Searches Run powerful Splunk queries to extract insights and drive intelligent workflows. - Leverage AI capabilities from Splunk’s AI Assistant for SPL & MLTK SPL search generation from natural language, search optimization, search explanation, retrieve MLTK models and algorithms.

item.title: SPLap - Motorsport Telemetry Lab - v2.3.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
SPLap 2.3.0 makes the real race easier to share, easier to follow and quieter on the network. No changes to data, searches, dashboards, tokens, sourcetypes, imports or the canonical schema. Position Worm: Save image. The whole race as a PNG drawn in your browser, with the session title, the race stats and the wordmark, ready to post. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. Incident Review: What happened next. Under every event, the later race-control messages that name the same cars (noted, under investigation, penalty, penalty served). Click one to open it. Same loaded rows, no extra search. Labs: the Monza challenge. Three questions on the real session with deep links into Lap Delta (NOR lap 48 against PIA lap 47), the Position Worm (the lap 45 and 46 McLaren stops) and Incident Review (lap 42, Turn 5), plus a send-your-answer mail link and a link to splap.dev/monza. Both open only when clicked. Pit Wall: jump to any lap inside the replay window from the timeline, and ?attract\=1 and ?broadcast\=1 deep links for kiosk and floor demos. Fast Lap Tour: six steps, starting on the Position Worm. The incident and lap-comparison steps now open the real 2025 Italian GP session instead of the synthetic fixture. An honest rating ask. After real use (a few Show SPL opens across views, three analysis views, a finished Fast Lap Tour or a completed import; never on first launch) one small card asks whether SPLap earned a Splunkbase rating, with Report a problem given equal weight. Not now snoozes it for 30 days and it stops after two. Remembered in this browser only; nothing is sent anywhere. About and Support: a rate-or-report panel, a disclaimer that describes the bundled OpenF1 session accurately, provenance for the Monza session and the real session in the header. Connect Data now explains "no imports yet" in plain words. Install Doctor: the optional OpenF1 connectivity check is click-to-run (or ?probe\=1), so the app makes no external request on its own and an air-gapped install no longer waits on a timeout it cannot fix.


Short Description:
Learn Splunk by replaying a real Formula 1 Grand Prix. Open the app and the 2025 Italian GP is already moving: 20 cars, a timing tower, real telemetry and the SPL behind every panel. Free, no API key, no internet, no LLM.


Description:
Install one free app and a real Formula 1 race is already moving inside Splunk. SPLap replays the 2025 Italian Grand Prix from real telemetry: 20 cars on a Monza map drawn from their own GPS, a timing tower with live gaps, every driver's speed, throttle, brake and gear, and race-engineer findings computed in SPL. Every panel has a Show SPL button, so the query behind what you are watching is one click away. A Grand Prix is a better SPL tutorial than another security log. Pit Wall The race replaying at broadcast pace, from 0.25x to 4x. Pick a driver, scrub to any lap, jump to the next pit stop, overtake or flag, or let Attract Mode drive and the battles find you. Share Moment copies a link to the exact second. Position Worm The whole race on one canvas: all 20 drivers across all 53 laps, pit stops dotted, safety-car periods shaded. Click any moment and the replay jumps there. Save image gives you the chart as a PNG to post. Lap Delta Any two laps aligned by distance, corner by corner: braking point, minimum speed, throttle reapplication and the time gained or lost. Try Norris lap 48 against Piastri lap 47 and find the 0.207 s. Incident Review A 30-second evidence window around any race-control message, overtake or pit stop, with both cars on the map and their telemetry on one cursor. What happened next adds the stewards' trail for the same cars. Make your own call on lap 42, Turn 5. Race Engineer Ten deterministic rules (pit-loss anomalies, undercuts and overcuts, tyre degradation steps, closing rates, braking-point changes and more), each finding with a confidence, provenance, evidence and the SPL that reproduces it. No language model anywhere. Bring your own race Connect Data imports any historical session from the community OpenF1 API in your browser, loads an offline race bundle on an air-gapped host, or runs from a Python CLI. Imported sessions get every view Monza gets. Runs anywhere Nothing to configure for the bundled race: no setup page, no API key, no index, no token, no internet after install. Splunk Enterprise 10.x or Splunk Cloud Platform, AppInspect passed for both. About 4 MB. Free and non-commercial. Made on weekends by Lloyd Clark and his daughter Lilli, two F1 nerds who wanted a better way to learn Splunk. Site, engineering notes and the Monza challenge: https://splap.dev SPLap is an independent project, not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Splunk LLC, Formula One Licensing BV, the FIA, any team, driver or circuit. Race data courtesy of OpenF1 under its non-commercial terms; no official logos, sponsor graphics or car images are used and team colours are curated approximations.

item.description:

Release Notes:
* The ValueSetter module can now switch on the job keys that only settle once a search has finished, for example `$results.count$` in an `if.*` param. Previously a ValueSetter like `if.$results.count$=0` evaluated only once, so it permanently reported the initial value. Such a module now waits for the job to finish before pushing to its downstream modules. Keys that are meant to be read while a search is still running, like `$results.doneProgress$`, are unaffected and continue to push immediately, as does `$results.fields$`, which comes from the Fields module rather than from the job. * Fixed a bug in the parsing of search expressions, when a tab or a newline character was read as part of the field name next to it, rather than as the token separator that SPL treats it as. A search filter of " foo\=bar" would give you a field name with a tab character in it, and any SPL built from that field name was then invalid. * Canary no longer reads the operating system certificate store when it asks splunkd for search job status. On a machine that has a truncated or corrupt cert in the store, this problem caused every page used to silently stop updating. * Improved messaging to the user if our job status poller's python handler hits an unexpected exception. * Job status polling now keeps its connection to splunkd open between polls instead of negotiating a new TLS session for every one. This only takes about 3ms off each poll but in aggregate from many users it's worth doing.

Release Notes:
## Release notes — v1.1.1 **Enhancement release on the 1.1.x line** — targets Splunk Enterprise / Cloud 10.2+ (Python 3.13). Same fix backported to the 1.0.x maintenance line as v1.0.8. ### What changed The WithSecure Elements API now returns a top-level `mitre` array on each BCD detection that mixes ATT\&CK tactic IDs (TA\*) and technique IDs (T\*), e.g. `["TA0003", "T1518.001", "T1543.002", "T1059.004"]`. Previously only the `activityContext[].mitre_id` items were populated for cloud detections and the flattened `ac_mitre_id` field was aliased to `mitre_technique_id`. Two new search-time EVAL calculated fields on the `withsecure:epp:bcd_detection` sourcetype split the flat array by prefix: ``` EVAL-mitre_technique_id = coalesce(mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^T[0-9]")), ac_mitre_id) EVAL-mitre_tactic_id = mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^TA[0-9]")) ``` The regexes are disjoint: `TA0003` matches `^TA[0-9]` but not `^T[0-9]` because `[0-9]` requires a digit at position 1, and `A` is not a digit. `mitre_technique_id` falls back to the legacy `ac_mitre_id` when the top-level array is not present, so events indexed before the API migration keep working. `mitre_tactic_id` is a new field aligned with the Splunk CIM Endpoint datamodel, no legacy fallback needed. ### SOC-friendly queries this enables ``` index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_tactic_id="TA0003" index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_technique_id IN ("T1059.001","T1112") index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" | stats count by mitre_tactic_id mitre_technique_id ``` ### Upgrade safety Non-destructive in-place upgrade. Search-time only — no ingestion impact, applies retroactively to detections already in the index, 100 % reversible.


Short Description:

item.title: Riskability - v1.2.3 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Riskability 1.2.3 Everything since 1.0.2, which is the version currently on this listing. 1.2.1, 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 add what is listed at the end. Only the changes that matter to somebody running the app are listed. ## A page about one machine Host detail gathers what the app knows about a single system, built as a dossier rather than a smaller copy of the fleet page. Identity and four clocks in one card: when the collector last ran, when the software last changed, when the host was last compared to the feed, and how old the feed is. Then an assessment ledger of what has been measured and what has not, what to do first, the open findings, the configuration surface the machine is set up to run, what it exposes, its Windows patch level, and what on it is no longer supported. The ledger is deliberately not a score. Its inputs are missing at unrelated rates, so a score would have to treat missing as zero, which is forbidden, or normalise over what is present, which is monotone the wrong way: the fewer things measured about a host, the better it would score. ## When nobody is going to fix it again The bundle now carries product and operating system support lifecycles, so the app can report software that has run out of supported releases. This is a different question from a CVE and no advisory answers it. Support is decided by who ships the copy. A package a distribution installs and maintains is informational while that distribution still supports its release, because vendors backport without changing the upstream version. A package carrying an esm or fips marker in its version string says in its own version that it is being maintained past the ordinary date. A copy no package manager owns is where the upstream date is the whole truth, and only that is reported at high confidence. A timeline on the Coverage page places every product release found on the fleet at the date its support ends, with everything already past that date included, because a product nobody has fixed for three years is the urgent end of the same timeline. Every row also states how much evidence there is that the software runs, from listening on a routable address down to installed with nothing observed running it. That order ranks evidence, not danger. Clicking a product on the timeline lists every host carrying it, and a row there opens that machine's own page. The lifecycle source is offered on both feed paths: a checkbox on the direct fetch in Feed administration, and a --lifecycle-file flag for a copy downloaded on a machine with better connectivity. Lifecycle data describes applications, runtimes, databases, servers and operating system releases rather than every library a distribution ships, so it covers a minority of any inventory and the Coverage page says so. ## Windows patch level, from Microsoft's own data A Windows host can now be told which build the vendor currently ships for its release, which update produces that build, and how many revisions behind it is. Windows 11 25H2 shipping as an enablement package over 24H2, and build 26100 being both Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025, are both handled explicitly. The panel says current with the feed rather than up to date, and means it: the comparison is inside the host's own servicing branch and edition, so it is never a claim that the release itself is the newest one or is still supported. ## The Riskability Cycle The landing page shows what the app is doing right now and what it does next. Almost every schedule in Riskability runs hourly, so the panel is a dial: one turn is one cycle of the pipeline. The centre names the next job and counts down to it, the hand marks where in the hour you are, and the lit arc covers the stretch the app is actually working, which on a default install is :05 to :55. Around the ring is a mark for each scheduled job at its own minute, coloured by how it last finished, and naming itself, its minute and its last duration when hovered. They are deliberately texture rather than a list: which of thirty six runs next matters far less than whether the cycle is turning at all, and a failure shows as a red mark on the ring without needing to be picked out by name. The two schedules that are not hourly cannot sit on an hour dial, so they are named underneath with when they next run rather than being left out. The panel refreshes every minute, so the countdown is live without reloading the page. It reads Splunk's own REST endpoints for the schedules and their last runs, and needs no access to any index, so it works for an account that can see the app but not the internal logs. An account that cannot see the schedules at all is told so, rather than being shown an idle pipeline. ## Hosts that are quiet on purpose A host that has not reported for a month is not necessarily broken. Some are collected only after a deliberate change. The app now learns each host's own reporting rhythm and calls it late only against that, rather than against a fixed threshold. Learned rhythms in testing ranged from hourly to once every sixty two days. Hosts that had gone quiet were previously deleted from the app outright and are now kept. ## Findings that were never real Installer and launcher stubs were catalogued as the software they install, producing findings about software that was not present. Load evidence could cross root boundaries, matching a snap base's library against the host's copy of the same name. On Windows a doubled backslash in a path meant a package could never be recognised as fixed, so an upgraded package stayed open forever. Open findings on the test fleet fell from 5,340 to 2,688, and none of the difference was a vulnerability that stopped being reported. A finding is also closed only when the source that reported it actually ran again. A collector invoked with a narrower set of sources no longer reads as software having been removed. ## Colour that means the same on every chart Chart colour was relative to whatever was on screen, so a fleet whose worst case was four findings and one whose worst case was four thousand drew the same picture. Colour is now an absolute scale, and a pale chart is a statement rather than an accident. ## Tables Date columns take a real range: an exact day, since, before, a span such as 2026-08-01..2026-08-28, and open ended forms such as 2026-08-01 followed by two dots. Columns whose values are typed rather than chosen no longer offer a dropdown of every value in the column. Advisories that never received a CVE number, such as GHSA, USN, DSA and RHSA identifiers, are links rather than plain text. ## Upgrading Replace the app and reload. No configuration changes and nothing to do on the forwarders or the indexers. The Windows patch level and end of support panels are populated by the next feed you import and say so until then, rather than implying that everything is current and supported. ## Corrections in 1.2.1 The support timeline's look ahead window and product picker are inside that panel now, rather than in a filter bar that implied it filtered the whole page. Every source in a bundle declares itself in the sources table on Feed administration. Windows update history registered nothing before, so a bundle carrying Microsoft build data did not say so and its attribution was recorded nowhere. The lifecycle source is named for its publisher, endoflife-date, like every other row there. ## Corrections in 1.2.2 Feed administration reported the Windows update source as unreachable when it was not. Every source was probed with an HTTP HEAD request, and Microsoft's update index answers HEAD with 405 Method Not Allowed while answering the request the builder actually makes with 200. Anyone reading that would have concluded Windows patch data could not be fetched and left it out. A source that refuses HEAD is now asked again the way the real fetch asks. ## Corrections in 1.2.3 A host is now kept for 180 days without contact rather than 30. That setting, `riskability_host_retire_days`, is the only thing deciding how long silence is tolerated, and a month deleted exactly the estates this app is built for: an appliance or OT fleet collected once a quarter lost every host between scans and was rediscovered later as new machines with no history. Lower it if your hosts report nightly, raise it for an annual audit cycle. Three tiles on the landing page stopped colouring themselves as faults. Newest inventory turned amber after six hours and red after forty eight, which tells a fleet collected twice a week that it is failing while it does exactly what it was configured to do. Last match climbed for ever on a stable fleet, because nothing is compared when nothing new has arrived, so it went red for having nothing to do. Open findings was amber above one finding and red above a hundred, which is every real fleet, permanently. All three are answered properly elsewhere: whether a host is late is judged against its own learned rhythm, and whether the pipeline is running is shown directly by the cycle dial. Feed age keeps its colour, because a stale feed does degrade every answer on every page no matter how often anybody scans. A host that reports rarely no longer disappears. Three views rebuilt themselves from a thirty day window and replaced their contents wholesale, so a machine quieter than that dropped out of the end of support view, the Windows patch level and the ecosystem coverage panel entirely, and the page then read as an answer rather than as missing data. They now carry their state forward like the rest of the app, and a single setting, riskability_host_retire_days, decides how long a silent host is kept. It defaults to thirty days and a site whose hosts report quarterly should raise it. There is no minimum collection frequency, and the Details tab now says so along with the smallest flag set the app can use. This matters for appliance and OT estates that are collected only after a deliberate change, which are a first class case here rather than an edge case. The feed builder can also be handed a source that the search head cannot download. Feed administration previously told anyone blocked from CISA to rebuild the entire bundle offline, which meant downloading every other source again over one file. A blocked source can now be uploaded on the page and the direct fetch uses it while downloading the rest as normal.


Short Description:
Correlate the software your fleet already reports against offline CVE databases on a search head with no internet access. Ranks findings by exploitation likelihood and by whether the network can actually reach them. Track software that is already or soon becoming End Of Life!


Description:
Most vulnerability tooling cannot run where it is needed most. A search head with no route to the internet cannot call an API, pull a feed on a schedule, or fetch a score on demand. Riskability is built for that machine. It takes the software inventory your hosts already report, correlates it against vulnerability databases you carry across the air gap yourself, and answers what a CVE count never does: of everything found, what should somebody actually do tonight? THE PROBLEM A fleet of any size produces tens of thousands of open findings. Severity alone does not reduce that to a working list. CVSS describes how bad a vulnerability would be if exploited, not how likely anyone is to exploit it, and neither knows whether your copy is reachable. WHAT THIS APP ADDS Exploitation likelihood. Findings are ranked by EPSS, the published probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild, and by the CISA KEV catalogue of vulnerabilities already observed under exploitation. Both arrive in the feed you import, never fetched live. Reachability. The collector reports listening ports, the process holding each one, and the containers behind them. Riskability separates findings that answer a network address from those that answer only loopback, and from those with nothing listening at all. On a test fleet that turned 10,206 open findings into 11 that answer the network. It reorders the work. It never shortens it. End of support. A CVE says a thing is broken. End of support says nobody is going to fix it again, which no advisory states. Product and operating system lifecycles ride in the same bundle, so the app names software that has run out of supported releases, places each on a timeline at the date support ends, and says how much evidence there is that it runs. One machine at a time. A host page gathers what is known about a single system: what has been measured on it and what has not, what it runs, what it exposes, and its Windows patch level. WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS Every finding carries a confidence level, and confidence describes the strength of the evidence rather than the severity of the vulnerability. Ubuntu and Red Hat backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so a version comparison alone cannot settle whether such a package is patched. Riskability reports that as informational and says why. The same rule governs end of support: a package a distribution still maintains is not called abandoned because its upstream series finished. A Coverage dashboard lists what the imported data cannot speak to at all, because a gap in visibility is not an absence of risk. Accepted risks are recorded in an audit index that is written once and never rewritten: who accepted, when, why, and when the acceptance expires. NO OUTBOUND NETWORK ACCESS The app makes no outbound requests. You build a feed bundle on a connected machine with the builder the app hands you, carry it across, and import it. Nothing is scheduled at install time.

Description:
AWS DFD Visualizer (Splunkbase App Summary) Purpose & Background Auditing complex cloud infrastructure for compliance (e.g., DoD Impact Level 5 (IL5), NIST 800-53, or NIST 800-207 Zero-Trust Architectures) is extremely challenging. While AWS accounts generate high-volume telemetry from AWS Config, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty, reviewing these complex configurations in standard tabular logs or flat Splunk tables makes it difficult for security teams, system auditors, and DevSecOps engineers to analyze isolation boundaries, spot structural gaps, or verify access routes. The Solution The AWS DFD (Data Flow Diagram) Visualizer solves this by transforming raw relationship logs and configuration items into interactive, visual security topologies styled after AWS Application Composer. It gives compliance officers and analysts an intuitive, visual framework to audit security posture in real-time. Key Features: Zero-Trust Layout Engine: Segregates assets deterministically into distinct swimlanes—separating the Identity plane (users/roles), Policy & Control plane (global network assets like WAF/CloudFront), and Infrastructure plane (VPCs/Subnets). Nested Enclosures: Renders nested container boundaries representing VPCs and Subnets with real-time compliance validation markers. Security & Telemetry Overlays: Highlights Security Group associations as outer compliance rings around compute nodes (Green for compliant, Red for non-compliant). Automatically isolates and flashes incident-flagged resources in pulsing red alerts. Overrides critical Nessus/Tenable vulnerability states with a custom "skull" threat icon. Dynamically intercepts and highlights non-compliant connection paths (e.g., SSH/22 path violations) as dashed Vibrant Red links. Dashboard Studio & SimpleXML Ready: Integrates natively with Splunk Dashboard Studio, supporting dynamic click-capturing drilldown tokens, responsive light/dark themes, and performance-saving Level of Detail (LOD) controls. Export & Live Console Feed: Includes a native client-side SVG/PNG exporter, a standard draw.io XML generator, and an ad-hoc CSV console feed for drafting cloud topologies on the fly. 🛠️ Configuration & Code Updates Done: To align your app bundle with this new description, I have updated the description strings in the following files: package.json splunk-app-manifest.json default/app.conf Additionally: Added /cypress/screenshots/ to .gitignore to keep the repository clean of test artifacts. Release Notes:
## Version 2.0.0 **Important — action required after upgrading.** Data inputs configured in v1.1.2 or earlier will no longer be listed on the Inputs page after this upgrade and must be recreated. Configured accounts, credentials and add-on settings are retained and do not need to be re-entered. ### Breaking change: modular input types renamed All modular input types are now prefixed with `vectra_rux_`: | Previous (v1.1.2 and earlier) | v2.0.0 and later | | --- | --- | | `entity_scoring_input` | `vectra_rux_entity_scoring_input` | | `detections_input` | `vectra_rux_detections_input` | | `audits_input` | `vectra_rux_audits_input` | | `lockdown_input` | `vectra_rux_lockdown_input` | | `health_input` | `vectra_rux_health_input` | Earlier releases used generic input-type names that other Splunk technology add-ons can also define. Modular input names are unique per Splunk instance, so where another add-on defined the same name, Splunk could load the wrong input definition or return an error on the Inputs page. Prefixing every Vectra input type guarantees these definitions are unique. Splunk treats the renamed types as new inputs, which is why data inputs created in v1.1.2 or earlier are not carried forward. ### New features * **Detection input** — added `Include Triaged`, `Include Info Category` and `From Checkpoint ID`. `From Checkpoint ID` lets collection begin from a specific detection event ID on the first run. * **Health input** — added optional collection of EDR and external connector health data: `Get Health EDR`, `Get Health EDR Details`, `Get Health External Connectors` and `Get Health External Connectors Details`. Each dataset is ingested with its own `source` value so it can be searched independently. ### Changes * Detection, audit and lockdown collection migrated to Vectra RUX API v3.5. Health and entity scoring collection continues to use v3.4. * Entity scoring collects from the unified `/entities` endpoint using page-based pagination. * The add-on version reported to the Vectra API is now read from `app.conf` at runtime, so it stays accurate across releases. * Refreshed Vectra branding for the app icon and navigation logo. ### Upgrade procedure 1. Record the configuration of each existing data input (name, interval, index and Vectra RUX account). 2. Disable & delete all configured inputs. 3. Install the v2.0.0 package with the **Upgrade app** option selected. 4. Restart Splunk. A restart is required for this release. 5. Recreate each data input from the Inputs page using the values recorded in step 1. Existing checkpoints are preserved. Recreating an input with the same name resumes collection from where it stopped, avoiding gaps and duplicate events. ### Documentation * [Upgrade guide: v1.1.2 to v2.0.0](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/upgrade-guide-vectra-xdr-technology-add-on-v1.1.2-to-vectra-rux-technology-add-on-v2.0.0) * [Splunk On-Prem integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux) * [Splunk Cloud integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux-1) ### Support Email [support@vectra.ai](mailto:support@vectra.ai)

item.title: Adjutant AI (AI Workbench) - v2.4.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-26 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.4.0** — a connectivity release on top of **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.4.0 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. Both stalled in the same place. The credentials were right, the firewall was open, the built-in connection test was green — and every question still failed. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. Where the service lists its deployments, it also shows you every deployment it found together with the model behind each one, which answers a question customers ask constantly: the deployment is named `gpt-4o`, but is that actually what runs? It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. When it cannot finish the job it says exactly what is still missing instead of failing vaguely — most usefully "the address and version are confirmed, the deployment name is not", which turns a five-part question for the API team into a one-part question. It also recognises a service that speaks the OpenAI dialect rather than the Azure one, and tells you to change provider instead of leaving you to guess. It runs only when you press it, and it is capped so it cannot flood anyone's gateway. ### Test connection now reports on the address, not just the login The connection test could report success on a configuration that no question would ever work against. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. That combination sent at least one administrator hunting through firewall rules for an afternoon. It now reports the two things separately. When the address does not work it says so plainly, and distinguishes the two reasons — an address that was left as the service base, or a deployment name that does not exist. When everything is right, it names the model that answered. ### Proxy exceptions, per configuration Reaching Microsoft to sign in and reaching the AI service are two different destinations, and in a locked-down network they often need opposite treatment: the corporate proxy is the only way out to Microsoft, while the service itself answers only on a direct connection. Until now a configuration had one proxy setting for both, so whichever you chose broke the other, and the only workaround changed proxy behaviour for every Splunk process on the machine. Configurations that use a proxy can now list the hosts that must bypass it. Sign-in goes through the proxy, the AI service is reached directly, nothing else on the server is affected, and the change takes effect when you save rather than when you restart. ### Fixed - **Model discovery found nothing behind an API gateway.** The lookup rebuilt the address from the hostname alone and threw away the path prefix, so it asked the wrong place and quietly reported no models. It now keeps the prefix. - **Deployments with your own naming lost their cost figures.** A deployment named for your estate rather than for the model — `acme-gpt4o-prod` — is not a name the price list knows, so usage was recorded with no money against it. The model that actually answered is now recorded alongside the configured name and used for pricing when the configured name is unknown, so those deployments cost correctly. Where the two differ, both are kept. - **A licence that could never be activated said "re-activate".** A key issued with no device limit records no activations at all, so a node-locked tier can never be satisfied by it and pressing re-activate cannot help. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Install once on the Search Head, then embed it in the apps your users already live in — Search, ITSI, Enterprise Security, your SOC and MSP customer apps. Users never leave the app they came from, and artefacts land in that app's namespace. Ask in plain English. Get back validated SPL, Simple XML and Dashboard Studio dashboards, alerts, lookups, reports and Splunk AI Toolkit (MLTK) machine-learning pipelines — grounded in your running Splunk (your knowledge objects, live command syntax, CIM models), run for real before they are saved, owned by the calling user. The depth is the difference. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. The Fraud Data Coverage Audit grades your estate against nine use cases (including AML) and returns ready, partial or blocked with the specific blocker, identifying event families by what events contain rather than by sourcetype name. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. A red KPI on a dead feed is a data problem, and it names the forwarder, HEC, DB Connect, Cribl or Edge Processor leg at fault. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Free, Professional, Enterprise and MSP tiers, self-serve and air-gap-friendly.

Short Description:
The NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer Add‑on maps Omnis Streamer data into Splunk, enabling faster analysis and custom dashboards. The Omnis Streamer App on Splunkbase leverages this mapping to accelerate insights.


Description:
The NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer Add‑on enables Splunk administrators to map NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer data into Splunk. NETSCOUT also provides the NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer App on Splunkbase, which leverages this data mapping to accelerate analysis and support the creation of customized dashboards. Note: The NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer CIM Add‑on and the NETSCOUT Omnis Streamer Add‑on should not be installed on the same Splunk system.
